newsitem.title: USA: U.S. CREDIT OUTLOOK - Calm, but waiting for retail.
newsitem.headline: U.S. CREDIT OUTLOOK - Calm, but waiting for retail.

text.p: Economic events in the next couple of days should do little to shake the positive sentiment that crept back into the U.S. credit markets during Monday's rebound, analysts said.
With no top-tier economic reports scheduled for Tuesday, the market should keep a steady tack at least until inflation data later in the week, they said.
"We're just correcting that big downward move of last week," said Josh Stiles, senior bond strategist at I.D.E.A. Inc.
Although surprises seem unlikely, market players will take a close look at a couple of reports on Tuesday.

The first is the BTM/Schroders report on chain store sales for the first week of December, scheduled for release at 0900 EST/1400 GMT. Skewed seasonal factors resulted in a 0.2 percent decline last week, but an increase in sales should be apparent in this week's release, analysts said.

The Redbook Research report on early December retail sales is also due Tuesday. But some analysts believe Redbook historically has understated sales for the first week of December, making BTM/Schroders report more relevant this week.
"We should start to see the pickup in sales showing up in the weekly reports to corraborate all the anecdotal evidence we've seen," said Stiles.

Data reflecting a seasonal surge should not surprise investors, most analysts said. "The market is primed for a big number" in the BTM/Schroders report, said Carey Leahey, senior vice president and senior financial markets economist at Lehman Government Securities Inc.
But some analysts said an exceedingly strong figure could prompt selling, even though a clear picture of holiday retail activity is a few weeks off.

David Jones, chief economist at Aubrey G. Lanston & Co Inc, predicted that holiday sales could improve "in the 7.0 to 8.0 percent range year-over-year" from a weak 1995. "You get into that territory and the markets will start to notice," he added.
Other Tuesday reports appear fairly insignificant for the credit markets, analysts said.
At 1000 EST/1500 GMT, the Commerce Department will report on October wholesale inventories and the U.S. current account balance for the third-quarter.

Also at 1000 EST/1500 GMT, the Federal Reserve Bank of Richmond will release the results of its November survey of business conditions. In October the shipments component rose to 4.0 from 2.0 and the services index rose to 17.0 from -2.0.

The markets have recovered since being rocked early Friday after Federal Reserve Chairman Alan Greenspan warned against "irrational exuberance" in asset markets. "The market is reevaluating the significance of what Greenspan said and is feeling less threatened by it," Stiles said. "If it did carry more weight, in the market's mind, it was toward the stock side rather than the bond side."
Having passed through that turbulence, the 30-year bond yield is seen in a trading range of about 6.25 to 6.50 percent this week -- and possibly through the end of this year, analysts said.
